source.title_on_document: Empowering Engineering Students Through Artificial Intelligence (AI): Blended Human–AI Creative Ideation Processes With ChatGPT

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is referenced in the document; the PDF ends with references on p. 19.
supplement.holds: No supplement identified. The direct assistance comparison is shown graphically in Figure 7 (p. 11); numerical test results in Table 4 (p. 11) instead concern prior ChatGPT experience.

paper_design_summary: Third-year industrial design and product development engineering students were randomly assigned to opposite orders of ChatGPT-assisted and unaided ideation, switching conditions between a public-transport task and a university-spaces task (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). The analyzed cohort comprised 51 students and produced 728 sketched and briefly described ideas; students subsequently assessed peers' ideas for creativity, innovation, viability, user benefits, value, complexity, and overall quality (p. 4, section 4.1; pp. 5 and 8, Table 1 and section 4.3.2; pp. 14 and 16, sections 6-7). A non-randomized comparison of previous ChatGPT experience uses the same study's AI-assisted outputs (pp. 9 and 11, section 5 and Table 4).

studies.label: Controlled crossover experiment: public transport and university-space ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly assigned to groups determining assistance order. Group A completed T1 without ChatGPT and T2 with ChatGPT; Group B completed T1 with ChatGPT and T2 without ChatGPT. Task order was fixed, while AI-condition order was randomized. Prior ChatGPT experience, examined separately in Table 4, was not assigned.
assignment.quote: For the experiment, students were randomly assigned to two groups and placed in classrooms based on their respective group assignments:
assignment.locator: pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1; p. 11, Table 4 for the experience subgroups

arms.name: ChatGPT-assisted ideation
arms.description: Experimental condition: supervised use of ChatGPT on university-provided computers; other websites and tools restricted. Group B receives this condition in T1 and Group A in T2. These are condition labels, not independent groups of people across both tasks (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1).

arms.name: Unaided ideation
arms.description: Control condition: supervised ideation in a computer-free classroom without external support. Group A receives this condition in T1; Group B receives it in T2 after its earlier ChatGPT use (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1).

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition are reported. The paper reports 51 participants and explicitly describes its results as deriving from this cohort, but gives no separate number at random assignment or per-sequence participant counts. Table 4 reports n = 80 and n = 280 ideas for its prior-experience comparison, not participant counts; its relation to the experimental-condition subtotal of 368 ideas in Table 3 is unexplained (pp. 4, 7, 11 and 16).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduates in the Bachelor's Degree in Engineering specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development at Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC); the participating students also evaluated peers' outputs (p. 4, section 4.1; p. 8, section 4.3.2; p. 16, section 7).
participants.country: Spain (university affiliations on p. 1; participant institution on p. 4)
participants.quote: The results of this research primarily derive from a cohort of 51 engineering students specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4.1; p. 16, section 7 (cohort underlying the results and 51 evaluators)

ai_tool.how_used: Students were instructed to use the text chatbot to support ideation. It answered questions, offered explanations and background information, and suggested directions for creative work; prompts were not standardized or reproduced. Access to other websites and tools was restricted (p. 7, section 4.3.1).

task.description: T1: generate innovative ideas to improve public transport. T2: generate innovative ideas to improve university spaces. Students were asked for eight unique ideas per task, each expressed as a sketch and brief description on an A5 template (p. 6, section 4.3.1).
task.duration: 30 min per task, with conditions and classrooms reversed after T1 (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1).

outcomes.name: Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Anonymous peer ratings by participating third-year students, excluding self-evaluation; raters were students rather than an independent expert panel. Items used a 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 4 (Strongly Agree) scale. Three items: Is creative; Solves the problem in an original way; Is unconventional. Cronbach's alpha = 0.83. Instrument and scale: p. 5, section 4.2.1 and Table 1; rating procedure: p. 8, section 4.3.2. Figure 7 reports this measure for T1, T2 and the total; exact plotted values and the meaning of error bars are not specified. The AI-assisted condition had ChatGPT available during production. Its T2 unaided comparator was produced after prior AI use, while its T1 comparator preceded any experimental AI exposure (pp. 6-7, Figure 1). The additional prior-experience contrast below is observational, uses AI-assisted ideas from the same experiment, and is not the randomized assistance effect (p. 11, Table 4).

contrasts.reported: The paper reports no significant differences in peer evaluations between ideas generated with and without ChatGPT (Mann-Whitney test). Figure 7 shows T1, T2 and total bars, but no exact numerical condition means, SDs, test statistics, p-values, or error-bar values are printed for this contrast. The text describes slightly higher scores with ChatGPT in T1 and higher scores without ChatGPT in T2 (p. 9, section 5).
contrasts.locator: p. 9, sections 4.4 and 5; p. 11, Figure 7; p. 14, section 6, Research question 2

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated (descriptive condition totals)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Table 3 counts submitted ideas by task and current condition. Figure 1 identifies the control row as without ChatGPT and the experimental row as with ChatGPT, with students changing rows between tasks. This is an aggregate output tally, not a tested participant-level fluency score. The instruction requested eight ideas within 30 min per task; person-level counts, means, SDs, and statistical tests of idea quantity are not reported (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1, Figure 1 and Table 3).

contrasts.reported: Table 3: experimental group, Task 1 = 195 ideas, Task 2 = 173, subtotal = 368; control group, Task 1 = 158, Task 2 = 202, subtotal = 360. Task subtotals = 353 and 375; total = 728 ideas. Descriptive direction reverses between tasks; no inferential quantity comparison is reported. In T2, the unaided control outputs follow prior AI use.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Table 3 and Figure 1; pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned to opposite orders of AI-assisted and unaided ideation (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). The results derive from 51 people, just above the eligibility threshold, rather than from 728 people; 728 is the number of ideas (p. 4, section 4.1; p. 7, Table 3; p. 16, section 7). Creativity and related dimensions were peer-rated on the actual ideas (p. 5, Table 1; p. 8, section 4.3.2; p. 14, section 6). The experiment is eligible despite the lack of numerical assistance-effect estimates and participant-adjusted precision. The prior-experience contrast in Table 4 is not randomized.

one_line_finding: Among 51 engineering students who generated 728 ideas, the paper reports no significant differences in peer-rated ideation outcomes with versus without ChatGPT (p. 16, section 7; p. 7, Table 3; p. 9, section 5; p. 11, Figure 7).
open_questions: The allocation method beyond random assignment, the number randomized, and the participant count in each sequence are not supplied (pp. 4 and 6-7, sections 4.1 and 4.3.1).

Figure 7 supplies no exact numerical means, SDs, test statistics, p-values, or defined error-bar values for the assistance contrast. Numeric values would require the data; the plotted bars were not digitized (pp. 9 and 11, section 5 and Figure 7).

The AI-assisted prior-experience analysis lists n = 80 and n = 280 ideas in Table 4, whereas Table 3 gives 368 experimental-condition ideas. The document does not reconcile these counts or report subgroup participant counts (pp. 7 and 11).
Mann-Whitney tests are described for idea evaluations, without reported participant clustering, paired/crossover adjustment, or a participant-level standard error (p. 9, section 4.4; p. 11, Table 4).

The T2 unaided outputs were produced after Group B lost ChatGPT access. No washout or separate carryover analysis is described, and no comparison with both groups working unassisted after different AI exposure is reported (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1; p. 11, Figure 7).
notes: The markdown was read from beginning to end, including all references; it contains no appendix. Relevant PDF text and the rendered figures/tables on pp. 7 and 11 were checked. This is one experiment with two tasks and a later rating session, not two independent samples. Coded lab_rct because the documented setting is a controlled, supervised session in separate classrooms; the article does not establish that this was ordinary coursework (pp. 6-8). Arms name the current assistance conditions; sequence membership reverses across tasks. The with_ai records describe the current-assistance comparisons in Figure 7, with its T1, T2 and total panels retained as variants of each measure. Specifically, the T2 unaided comparator is after_ai work, not an AI-naive control; the paper supplies no separate after_ai effect. Rating in the second session does not make the original production outcome delayed. The seven rated outcomes are recorded separately; the eighth outcome preserves the descriptive idea counts in Table 3, which are not a tested participant-level fluency effect. Complexity is coded other because it concerns interacting concepts and details, not simply output length. Overall assessment is coded usefulness because its item is Is a good idea, rather than an explicit overall-creativity rating (p. 5, Table 1). The observational prior-experience comparisons are retained as comparison_type other within the same outcome records; their means, SDs and r values must not be used as AI-versus-no-AI statistics. No standardized effect was computed. The n_units = 728 in each rated outcome refers to the complete peer-assessed idea corpus (p. 14, section 6); Table 4 subgroup idea counts are given separately. Self-reported perceptions and qualitative concerns about homogeneity are not scored diversity outcomes and were not entered as such (p. 6, Table 2; pp. 9-14, results and Table 5). No shared sample with another paper is stated. Data and materials are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request; no data or code URL is supplied (p. 17, Data Availability Statement).
